_note: Plain-language content per class in shared/conditions.yaml. Education only: no diagnosis, no medication advice.

calculus.label: Tartar (calculus)
calculus.short: Hardened plaque stuck to the teeth
calculus.what: Tartar is plaque that has hardened onto your teeth, usually along the gumline. It looks yellow or brown and you can't brush it off at home.
calculus.why: Plaque that stays on teeth for a few days hardens into tartar. It builds faster if you skip cleaning between teeth, smoke, or have sugary drinks often.
calculus.if_left: Tartar irritates the gums. Over months it can lead to gum disease, with bleeding, receding gums and, eventually, loose teeth.
calculus.dentist: A scaling and polishing visit removes it, usually in one appointment of about 30 minutes.
home: Brush twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste.
Clean between your teeth once a day with floss or interdental brushes.
Tartar won't come off at home, so plan a cleaning.

caries.label: Tooth decay (caries)
caries.short: A cavity: damage to the tooth's hard surface
caries.what: Tooth decay is damage to the tooth caused by acid from bacteria. Early decay looks like a chalky white or brown spot, and later becomes a hole (cavity).
caries.why: Bacteria in plaque turn sugar into acid, which slowly dissolves the tooth. Frequent snacking, sweet drinks and missed brushing speed this up.
caries.if_left: Decay doesn't heal by itself. It spreads inward and can reach the nerve, causing pain or infection. At that stage a filling may no longer be enough.
caries.dentist: A dentist checks how deep it goes. Small cavities are usually filled in one visit. Deeper decay may need a root canal and a crown.
home: Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, and spit rather than rinse afterwards.
Cut down on sweet drinks and snacks between meals.
Book a check soon: a small filling now costs much less than a root canal later.

hypodontia.label: Missing teeth (hypodontia)
hypodontia.short: One or more teeth may be missing
hypodontia.what: Hypodontia means one or more teeth never developed. A photo can't tell a tooth that never formed from one that was lost or hasn't come through yet. An X-ray can.
hypodontia.why: It is usually genetic and is often noticed in childhood or the teens. Teeth lost to decay, gum disease or injury can look similar in a photo.
hypodontia.if_left: It isn't harmful by itself. Over time, nearby teeth can drift into the gap, which can change your bite and make cleaning harder.
hypodontia.dentist: A dentist confirms it with an X-ray and talks you through options: leaving the gap, braces, a bridge, a denture or an implant.
home: Clean carefully around the gap; food tends to collect there.
Interdental brushes reach the sides of teeth next to a gap.

mouth_ulcer.label: Mouth ulcer
mouth_ulcer.short: A small sore inside the mouth
mouth_ulcer.what: A mouth ulcer is a small, painful sore on the inside of the cheeks, lips, tongue or gums. It is usually round, white or yellow, with a red edge.
mouth_ulcer.why: Common triggers are biting your cheek, a sharp tooth or brace, a hard toothbrush, stress, and some foods. Many people get them now and then.
mouth_ulcer.if_left: Most heal by themselves within one to two weeks. An ulcer that lasts longer than two weeks, keeps coming back, or is unusually large needs to be checked by a dentist or doctor.
mouth_ulcer.dentist: A dentist or doctor looks at the sore and asks how long you've had it. If it isn't healing, they may refer you for further checks.
home: Use a soft toothbrush and brush gently around the sore.
For a few days, avoid very spicy, acidic or rough foods.
Note the date you first noticed it. If it's still there after two weeks, get it checked.

tooth_discoloration.label: Tooth discolouration
tooth_discoloration.what: Discolouration is any change in tooth colour, such as yellow or brown staining, or a single tooth turning grey.
tooth_discoloration.why: Most staining sits on the surface and comes from tea, coffee, smoking or strongly coloured food. Deeper colour changes can follow an injury to a tooth, decay, or some childhood medicines.
tooth_discoloration.if_left: Surface staining is a cosmetic issue. A single tooth that has turned dark, especially after a knock, should be checked, as it can mean the nerve is affected.
tooth_discoloration.dentist: A scaling and polishing visit removes most surface stains. A dentist can also tell you whether the colour change is on the surface or deeper.
home: Rinse with water after tea, coffee or curry.
Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.
If one tooth has darkened after an injury, book a check sooner.

normal.label: No visible condition
normal.short: Nothing stood out in this photo
normal.what: None of the five conditions Gigi screens for stood out in this photo. That's a good sign, but it isn't a clean bill of health.
normal.why: A photo only shows surfaces the camera can see. Gum disease, decay between teeth and problems below the gumline need an in-person check.
normal.if_left: Keep up routine care. Up to 90% of adults in Singapore have some gum disease, and it is usually painless in the early stages.
normal.dentist: A routine check-up and cleaning every 6 to 12 months catches problems while they are small and cheap to fix.
home: Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.
Clean between your teeth once a day.
Bleeding gums aren't normal. Mention them at your next check-up.

routine.label: Routine
routine.advice: Book a dental visit in the next few months.

watch.label: Watch it
watch.advice: Keep an eye on it. See a dentist or doctor if it hasn't healed in two weeks.

soon.label: See a dentist soon
soon.advice: Book a dental visit within the next 2 to 4 weeks.

unsure.label: Not sure
unsure.advice: The photo wasn't clear enough to screen. Retake it, or ask a dentist to take a look.

emergency_signs: Swelling in your face, jaw or neck
Bleeding from the mouth that won't stop
A tooth knocked out or broken in an accident
Fever with a painful, swollen mouth
Difficulty breathing, swallowing or opening your mouth
